## Learning objectives

1. Choose the right Quarto output for a given audience: article, slides,
   website, thesis.
2. Split a long document into `include`d child files.
3. Use shortcodes, callouts and cross-references to structure a document.
4. Produce a journal-formatted manuscript with a `.bib` bibliography and a
   CSL style.
5. Publish a website to GitHub Pages.

## Yesterday you rendered a document. Today, a body of work.

The `.qmd` file you made at 14:45 yesterday scales, unchanged in principle,
to a thesis. What changes is organisation.

| Output | Format | For |
|---|---|---|
| Manuscript | `format: docx` (+ `pdf`) | Journals, co-authors |
| Slides | `format: revealjs` | Conferences, teaching |
| Website | `project: type: website` | Course sites, project pages, this site |
| Book / thesis | `project: type: book` | Long documents with chapters |
| Blog | `type: website` + `listing:` | Ongoing writing |
| Dashboard | `format: dashboard` | Monitoring, surveillance |

All from Markdown and R chunks you already know.

## Splitting a long document

A 12,000-word thesis chapter in a single `.qmd` is unmanageable. Break it up:

```
thesis/
├── index.qmd            # YAML, abstract
├── 01-introduction.qmd
├── 02-methods.qmd
├── 03-results.qmd
├── 04-discussion.qmd
├── references.bib
└── _quarto.yml
```

Or, within one document, pull in child files:

```markdown
{{< include _methods.qmd >}}
```

Files beginning with an underscore are not rendered on their own — exactly
what you want for a fragment.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Why this matters beyond tidiness
Each file is a unit you can hand to a co-author, track separately in version
control, and re-render alone while drafting. A 40-second render becomes 4
seconds, which is the difference between rendering constantly and avoiding it.
:::

## Shortcodes

Small `{{< >}}` directives that expand at render time:

| Shortcode | Does |
|---|---|
| `{{< include _file.qmd >}}` | Insert another file |
| `{{< video url >}}` | Embed a video |
| `{{< pagebreak >}}` | Page break in Word/PDF |
| `{{< meta title >}}` | Reuse a YAML field in the text |
| `{{< kbd Ctrl-S >}}` | Render a keyboard key |

`{{< meta >}}` is quietly useful: define the study name once in the YAML and
refer to it everywhere, so a rename is a one-line change.

## Callouts

```markdown
::: {.callout-note}
## Ethical approval
Approved by the Institutional Ethics Committee (IEC/2026/041).
:::
```

Five types: `note`, `tip`, `warning`, `important`, `caution`. Add
`collapse="true"` to fold them — used all over this site for solutions.

## A manuscript that a journal will accept

```yaml
---
title: "Flipped classroom teaching and knowledge gain: a multicentre study"
author:
  - name: A. Nair
    orcid: 0000-0002-1825-0097
    affiliations:
      - name: Government Medical College, Thrissur
    email: nair@example.ac.in
    corresponding: true
  - name: B. Soman
    affiliations:
      - name: SET Team
abstract: |
  **Background.** ...
  **Methods.** ...
  **Results.** ...
keywords: [medical education, flipped classroom, reproducible research]
bibliography: references.bib
csl: vancouver.csl
format:
  docx:
    reference-doc: journal-template.docx
    number-sections: true
  pdf:
    documentclass: article
    geometry: margin=1in
    linenumbers: true
execute:
  echo: false
  warning: false
---
```

Three details that save real time:

- **`reference-doc:`** — point it at a Word file styled the way the journal
  wants, and every render inherits the fonts, margins and heading styles.
- **`csl:`** — download the journal's style from
  [zotero.org/styles](https://www.zotero.org/styles). Switching from Vancouver
  to APA after a rejection becomes a one-line change instead of an evening.
- **`linenumbers: true`** — most journals require them for review. Two words
  here, versus a manual pass in Word.

::: {.callout-note}
## The Quarto manuscript project
`quarto create project manuscript` scaffolds a project designed for journal
submission: article, notebooks, and a website version from one source. Worth
exploring after this workshop. See
[quarto.org/docs/manuscripts](https://quarto.org/docs/manuscripts/).
:::

## Publishing a website

This site is a Quarto website. Its entire configuration is one `_quarto.yml`
with a navbar and a list of pages.

```bash
quarto publish gh-pages
```

One command: renders, pushes to a `gh-pages` branch, and gives you a public
URL. Free for public repositories. For a department page, a study protocol,
or teaching material, this is the shortest path from "I have a document" to
"colleagues can read it".

::: {.callout-warning}
## Before you publish anything
Rendered output can leak more than you intend: a `glimpse()` of an
unanonymised dataset, a file path containing a patient identifier, a raw CSV
sitting in `data/`. Check your `_site/` folder and your `.gitignore` before
the first push. Assume that anything pushed to a public repository is
permanent, because it effectively is.
:::

# Hands-on {#hands-on}

**10:15 – 11:00.** Work in your groups. One laptop drives; rotate every
15 minutes so everyone types.

::: {.callout-note title="Group exercise: build a dynamic document"}
**Time:** 45 minutes

Turn yesterday's `report.qmd` into a small structured manuscript.

1. Add a proper YAML header: title, at least two authors with affiliations,
   an abstract, and `format: html` plus `docx`.
2. Split it: move your setup chunk and data import into `_setup.qmd` and pull
   it in with `{{< include _setup.qmd >}}`.
3. Add sections: Background, Methods, Results, Limitations.
4. In Methods, state the missing-data decision you made yesterday — in prose,
   with the count reported through inline code.
5. Add one callout noting ethical approval (invent a number; this is
   synthetic data).
6. Cross-reference your figure with `@fig-gain`.
7. Render to both HTML and Word.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Skeleton to start from" collapse="true"}
````markdown
---
title: "Flipped classroom teaching and knowledge gain"
author:
  - name: "Group 1, Member A"
    affiliations: [{name: "Government Medical College, Thrissur"}]
  - name: "Group 1, Member B"
    affiliations: [{name: "Government Medical College, Kozhikode"}]
abstract: |
  Background. Flipped classroom methods are widely advocated but
  inconsistently evaluated. Methods. We compared knowledge gain in 240
  students across three colleges. Results. ...
format:
  html: {toc: true}
  docx: default
execute:
  echo: false
  warning: false
---

{{< include _setup.qmd >}}

## Background

...

## Methods

Data were collected from 240 students across three government medical
colleges. Post-test scores were unavailable for
`r knitr::inline_expr("sum(is.na(students$posttest))")` students, who are
excluded from all analyses of knowledge gain; no imputation was performed.

::: {.callout-note}
## Ethical approval
Institutional Ethics Committee approval IEC/2026/041. All data presented
here are synthetic and generated for training purposes.
:::

## Results

See @fig-gain.

## Limitations

...
````

`_setup.qmd` contains only:

````markdown
```{{r}}
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
students <- read_csv("data/meded_students.csv")
```
````
:::

## Key takeaways

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
- Same source, different `format:` — article, slides, website, thesis.
- Split long documents; prefix fragments with `_` and pull them in with
  `{{< include >}}`.
- `reference-doc:` and `csl:` turn journal reformatting into one line.
- `quarto publish gh-pages` puts it online in one command.
- Check what your rendered output reveals before you publish it.
:::
